content.text:
The file-types work is done, tested and committed (`9fc4775`).

**What the parser reads now**

| Type | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| **zip** | unreadable, flagged | each file inside is read as its own attachment, and lines name that file as their source |
| zip bombs, deep nesting, password-protected zips | — | refused or flagged, never unpacked |
| **.xlsx sent with the wrong or no extension** | unreadable | recognised by its contents |
| **old .xls** | unreadable | read like .xlsx, keeping hidden sheets/rows and struck-out cells |
| **iPhone HEIC photo** | unreadable | converted to JPEG and read |
| **sideways phone photo** (rotation tag) | sent sideways | turned upright first |
| **iPhone "MPO" JPEG** | would have been sent twice | treated as one photo |
| **.doc / Outlook .msg** | unreadable | still flagged for review, on purpose: I can't generate a test file for either, so I won't ship an untested reader |

**How I know it works**
- **12 new unit tests** build each file type on the fly. All 64 tests pass.
- **End to end:** I added 3 new emails to the stress inbox (a zip, a sideways photo, a HEIC photo) and wrote the expected answers *before* running. The live run cost $0.011, and all 3 came out right on classification, lines, quantities and sources.
- **No collateral damage:** a fresh copy installed from scratch replays dev and stress with no key, **byte-identical**. The changes didn't alter anything the model saw on existing emails, so every cached answer is still valid.

**What we learned along the way:** I nearly changed the prompt because the model wrote "socket weld" where the customer wrote "SW". I checked the dev answer key first, and its authors accept both spellings (`socket weld|sw`, on 37 lines). So the mistake was in *my* test's expectation, not the parser. Checking first saved a full re-run of every email and the risk of changing answers that were already right. That's a good interview moment.

**Next on our list: long PDFs in windows.** Instead of stopping at page 30, read the whole PDF in chunks, merge the lines, and still flag it for review. Ready to start?
yes

Here's the plan before I touch code.

**How it works today:** `ingest` reads the first 30 pages of a PDF, notes "only the first 30 of N pages", and the guards flag the email for review. In the stress test, a 35-page PDF loses its last 15 lines.

**The new design:**
1. Ingest reads every page, up to a hard cap of 300 (a 300-page spec book is the brief's own example).
2. If the email fits in one model call, nothing changes. Otherwise the pipeline makes **one call per window of 30 pages**. The first call classifies the email and reads the first window. Each later call reads only its window and is told the classification is already decided.
3. **The key risk is lost context.** A heading on page 2 ("ALL FLANGES 150# A105") may apply to rows on page 40. So every window also gets the document's first page and the last rows of the previous window, marked "context only: don't extract".
4. Each window is its own cached call, so re-runs stay free and repeatable.
5. A fully read document no longer needs review. Review is still forced if a window call fails or the PDF exceeds the 300-page cap.

I'll read the current PDF reader and pipeline to fit this in:

Here's the plan before I touch code.

**How it works today:** `ingest` reads the first 30 pages of a PDF, notes "only the first 30 of N pages", and the guards flag the email for review. In the stress test, a 35-page PDF loses its last 15 lines.

**The new design:**
1. Ingest reads every page, up to a hard cap of 300 (a 300-page spec book is the brief's own example).
2. If the email fits in one model call, nothing changes. Otherwise the pipeline makes **one call per window of 30 pages**. The first call classifies the email and reads the first window. Each later call reads only its window and is told the classification is already decided.
3. **The key risk is lost context.** A heading on page 2 ("ALL FLANGES 150# A105") may apply to rows on page 40. So every window also gets the document's first page and the last rows of the previous window, marked "context only: don't extract".
4. Each window is its own cached call, so re-runs stay free and repeatable.
5. A fully read document no longer needs review. Review is still forced if a window call fails or the PDF exceeds the 300-page cap.

I'll read the current PDF reader and pipeline to fit this in:

    """A later window of a long PDF, for its own call. The email is already classified; this call
    only reads lines. It also gets the document's first page and the end of the previous window
    as CONTEXT (a heading on page 2 can govern rows on page 40), marked not to be extracted."""
    w = part.windows[k]
    first_page = part.text.split("\n--- page 2", 1)[0]
    prev = part.text if k == 0 else part.windows[k - 1]["text"]
    tail = "\n".join(prev.splitlines()[-25:])
    names = ["body"] + [p.filename for p in em.parts]
    i = names.index(part.filename)
    text = (
        f"From: {em.sender}\nSubject: {em.subject}\n\n"
        f"This email is already classified as {classification}; its body and the earlier pages "
        f"were read separately. Attachment {i}: {part.filename!r} is long and is read in parts. "
        f"Below are pages {w['pages']} of it.\n"
        f"Return line_items ONLY for items on pages {w['pages']}, with source {part.filename!r}, "
        f"following all the usual rules. Set classification to {classification}. The CONTEXT "
        f"sections are for headings, notes and defaults that apply to these pages: never return "
        f"a line from CONTEXT.\n\n"
        f"=== CONTEXT: first page of the document ===\n{first_page}\n\n"
        f"=== CONTEXT: end of the previous part ===\n{tail}\n\n"

"""Run the inbox: ingest -> model (cached) -> guards, per email in parallel; then thread links.

Every email is isolated: any exception for one email becomes a flagged record for that email
and the run carries on. The run always writes a complete parsed.json.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import time
import traceback
from collections import Counter
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

from .guards import fallback, finalize, missing_rows
from .ingest import Email, load_email
from .llm import LLM, ModelUnavailable
from .matcher import load_catalog, match_all
from .prompt import INSTRUCTIONS, PROMPT_VERSION, REQUEST_CLASSES, build_input
from .threads import link


def process_one(path: Path, llm: LLM) -> tuple[Email, dict, dict]:
    stats = {"model_calls": 0, "cached": False, "usage": None, "cost_usd": 0.0, "seconds": 0.0, "warnings": [], "fallback": None}
    em = Email(id=path.stem)
    try:
        em = load_email(path)
        stats["warnings"] += em.errors
        content, schema, truncated = build_input(em)
        req = llm.request(INSTRUCTIONS, content, schema)
        res = llm.call(req, label=f"{PROMPT_VERSION}:{em.id}")
        _account(stats, res)
        record, warns = finalize(em, res.data, truncated)
        stats["model_reason"] = res.data.get("classification_reason")

        # Code checks completeness; the model gets one pointed second look (also cached).
        missed = missing_rows(em, record["line_items"]) if record["classification"] in REQUEST_CLASSES else {}
        if missed:
            listing = "\n".join(f"- from {f}: {r}" for f, rows in missed.items() for r in rows)
            stats["coverage_retry"] = listing
            note = (
                "CHECK: your previous answer did not include these numbered rows:\n" + listing +
                "\nRe-read the email. Return the complete answer again: include each of these rows "
                "if the customer is asking for it; leave a row out only if it is not requested "
                "(heading, crossed out, superseded, not among the accepted items)."
            )
            req2 = llm.request(INSTRUCTIONS, content + [{"type": "input_text", "text": note}], schema)
            try:
                res2 = llm.call(req2, label=f"{PROMPT_VERSION}:{em.id}:coverage")
                _account(stats, res2)
                record2, warns2 = finalize(em, res2.data, truncated)
                left = missing_rows(em, record2["line_items"])
                if record2["classification"] == record["classification"] and sum(map(len, left.values())) < sum(map(len, missed.values())):
                    record, warns, missed = record2, warns2, left
            except ModelUnavailable as e:
                warns.append(f"coverage retry failed: {e}")
            if missed:

    for part in em.parts:

"""Long PDFs are read in windows of pages, one cached model call each.

A fake model stands in for OpenAI, so these run offline and free. It answers each window with
the rows on that window's pages, and can be told to fail, to check that a lost window makes the
email need review instead of silently dropping its lines.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import Path

import pymupdf

from rfq.ingest import PDF_WINDOW_PAGES, load_email
from rfq.llm import CallResult, ModelUnavailable
from rfq.pipeline import process_one
from tests.test_ingest import _eml


def _pdf(pages: int) -> bytes:
    doc = pymupdf.open()
    for i in range(1, pages + 1):
        doc.new_page().insert_text((54, 72), f"{i} | 2 | EA | 2\" 150# RF slip-on flange, A105, item {i}", fontsize=10)
    return doc.tobytes()


class FakeLLM:
    """Answers with the numbered rows it can see in the PAGES section (or the first window)."""
    model, effort = "fake", "none"

    def __init__(self, fail_windows=False):
        self.fail_windows = fail_windows
        self.labels = []

    def request(self, instructions, content, schema):
        return {"content": content}

    def call(self, req, label=""):
        self.labels.append(label)
        text = "\n".join(c.get("text", "") for c in req["content"])
        window = "=== PAGES " in text
        if window and self.fail_windows:
            raise ModelUnavailable("provider down")
        if window:
            text = text.split("=== PAGES ", 1)[1]  # never the CONTEXT sections
        rows = re.findall(r"^(\d+ \| 2 \| EA \| .+)$", text, re.M)
        data = {"classification_reason": "asks for prices", "classification": "rfq", "needs_review": False,
                "review_reason": None,
                "line_items": [{"raw": r, "description": r.split(" | ")[-1], "qty": 2, "uom": "EA", "source": "big.pdf"}
                               for r in rows]}
        return CallResult(data, {"input_tokens": 1, "cached_input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 1, "reasoning_tokens": 0},
                          0.0, False, 0.0, key=label)


def test_short_pdf_is_one_window(tmp_path):
    (p,) = load_email(_eml(tmp_path, [("big.pdf", "application/pdf", _pdf(PDF_WINDOW_PAGES))])).parts
    assert p.windows == [] and "--- page 30" in p.text


def test_long_pdf_is_split_and_all_text_covers_every_page(tmp_path):
    (p,) = load_email(_eml(tmp_path, [("big.pdf", "application/pdf", _pdf(65))])).parts
    assert [w["pages"] for w in p.windows] == ["31-60", "61-65"]
    assert "item 1" in p.text and "item 31" not in p.text
    assert all(f"item {i}," in p.all_text for i in (1, 31, 65))
    assert any("not missing" in n for n in p.notes), "the model must be told the rest is read separately"


def test_every_window_adds_its_lines_once(tmp_path):
    llm = FakeLLM()
    _, rec, stats = process_one(_eml(tmp_path, [("big.pdf", "application/pdf", _pdf(65))]), llm)
    items = sorted(int(ln["raw"].split(" | ")[0]) for ln in rec["line_items"])
    assert items == list(range(1, 66)), "65 pages, 65 rows, none twice (CONTEXT is never extracted)"
    assert not rec["needs_review"]
    assert len(llm.labels) == 3 and stats["model_calls"] == 3


def test_a_window_that_cannot_be_read_flags_the_email(tmp_path):
    _, rec, _ = process_one(_eml(tmp_path, [("big.pdf", "application/pdf", _pdf(65))]), FakeLLM(fail_windows=True))
    assert rec["needs_review"] and "pages 31-60 could not be read" in rec["review_reason"]
    assert len(rec["line_items"]) == 30, "keep what was read"

# DECISIONS

**Time spent:** about 5 hours.

## Shape of the system — who decides what

`ingest` (code) → **one model call per email** (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, reasoning effort medium,
strict JSON schema) → `guards` (code) → `threads` (code) → `matcher` (code, optional part; see
[MATCHER.md](MATCHER.md): dev confident-wrong 0, not-in-catalog 16/16).

- **Code reads the files.** Every part becomes text or images before the model sees it: xlsx with
  sheet state, merged cells, hidden rows and struck cells marked; docx in document order with
  tracked deletions removed; PDF rows rebuilt from word positions, scans rendered to images;
  HTML tables flattened with `~~strike~~` kept. A broken part becomes `kind=unreadable` with a
  note — it never raises.
- **The model judges.** Classification, which lines are requests, and the self-contained
  description (heading scope, overrides beating defaults, quoted history is not a request).
  The prompt states principles, not dev strings; its one worked example is invented.
- **Code checks anything that is a fact.** Struck and hidden-only lines are dropped whatever the
  model said; non-request classes carry no lines; a request with zero lines, an unreadable part
  or a truncated document is always `needs_review`; `source` must be a real part; `raw` is
  snapped to the unique matching source row (the model's copy of a row varies run to run, and
  graders pair on `raw`). If a numbered table row is accounted for by no line, the model is
  asked once more with that row named (caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, $0.004).
- **Code links threads.** `revises` from In-Reply-To/References, then subject + sender domain;
  `duplicate_of` needs the same sender, ≤30 days, identical attachment hashes and matching lines.

**Measured, not guessed.** I wrote a scorer that implements the README's grading, and a
19-email stress inbox (`tests/stress/`) for situations dev doesn't show — tracked changes, a
Spanish request, a rotated photo, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a
byte-identical second delivery, a 35-page PDF. Its answers were written **before** running the
system. Dev: 24/24 classes, 210/210 lines, 0 silent / 0 hallucinated, context 172/173.
Stress: 19/19 classes, 118/133 lines (the 15 missing are pages 31–35, flagged), 0 hallucinated.
**Rejected:** gpt-5.5 — 4.6× the cost and *worse* on context (it "corrected" `A53B` to
`A53 Grade B`); a two-call classify-then-extract design — twice the cost, and the classifier
needs the same reading anyway.

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request. E013's bounce carries a
perfect numbered list of valves with quantities — it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier. E011 is a
supplier's price list. E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)` with the
superseded rows; a reader that loads every sheet quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the
filename calls it a revision although no earlier email exists. Meanwhile the real requests hide:
the spec is in a merged cell two rows above (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB UNLESS NOTED`) with
one row overriding it to SCH 80, or on a phone photo of a nameplate. So most of the accuracy came
from *ingest* — marking hidden, struck and merged structure faithfully — not from the prompt.

## Something in the brief or README you disagree with

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's own costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, an out-of-office from the buyer on a job with a deadline. Under the contract those come back
`auto_reply` / `other` with nothing to act on. **What I did:** kept the contract in
`parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because the grader scores it), and made the model state a
one-line reason for every classification; it is in `parsed.report.json` and the viewer, so a
person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate `attention`
field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 100% partly because I looked at it; the stress inbox (unseen until written) is the fairer
guide. For ~40 held-out emails: **silent losses 0** (every request with no lines is flagged by
code), **hallucinated lines 2–5**, **lost/phantom 1–2**, classification **~90%**, line recall
**~90%**, precision **~95%**, qty **~95%**, uom/source **~97%**, context carried **~85%**,
links mostly right, needs_review P/R **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt).

1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The reading is all we have, so a misread `6`/`8`,
   a missed line or a `raw` that pairs badly with the key's reading costs qty and recall. Code
   cannot check a picture; only the review flag helps, and the model flags too rarely.
2. **Terse revisions against an earlier email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the
   original list; when it's only partly quoted, the "complete order as now intended" will be
   incomplete or wrong. A second hazard on the same boundary: Rev B / resend / "also add" as new
   rfq vs revision — I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*", which held-out
   may draw differently.

## How this runs for real

**Built today:** content-addressed cache (sha256 of model + effort + prompt + full content incl.
image bytes, atomic writes), 3 retries with timeout, a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive
failures, a per-email header fallback, a 30-page cap, per-email isolation, and a per-email
cost/token report. **Not built:** the webhook, a queue, a database.

- **3,000 emails a day.** Measured cost is $0.0072 per email (3,940 tokens incl. reasoning) →
  about **$22/day**. Median latency 4.9 s, worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 per minute, so one worker
  keeps up. Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run
  `process_one`; thread linking moves from "whole inbox" to a lookup in a store of past emails by
  Message-ID, subject and domain.
- **Provider down for two hours.** Today: retries, then the breaker trips and every remaining
  email gets the fallback — headers decide auto_reply/bulk, everything else becomes
  `rfq` + `needs_review` ("not read automatically"). Fallbacks are not cached, so the next run
  calls the model for exactly those emails. For real I'd hold them in the queue with backoff
  for a while before handing them to people, with an alert — 250 emails to a person is worse
  than a 2-hour delay.
- **A 300-page PDF.** Today: the first 30 pages are read and the email is flagged
  "only the first 30 of 300 pages read" (stress S18). Next: split into page windows, one call each,
  merge lines, and still flag for review — a 300-page document is usually a spec book, not a list.
- **The same email delivered twice.** Built two ways: the second delivery hashes to the same
  cache key, so it costs nothing, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` the first
  (stress S13 is a byte copy). For real, dedupe on Message-ID + body hash at the webhook before
  any work.

## Known broken / next

- `raw` for pictures varies between runs (E023's nameplate); the cache makes it stable for
  replay, not right.
- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
- The matcher reads only our `description`, so a context miss in extraction becomes a matching
  miss (MATCHER.md lists its own weaknesses).
- Next: page-window chunking, an `attention` field, and using the viewer's rep overturns of
  matches as the matcher's running error rate.

content.text:
Long PDFs are done and committed (`7e13bfe`).

**What changed:** a long PDF used to stop at page 30, flag the email, and lose the rest. Now it's read in **windows** of 30 pages (or 16 scanned pages, because a call takes at most 20 pictures):
- The first window goes with the email as before. Each later window is its own cached call that only adds lines.
- Every window also gets the document's **first page** and the **end of the previous window**, marked "context only, don't extract". A heading on page 2 like "ALL FLANGES 150# A105" still applies to rows on page 40.
- If a window's call fails, the email is **flagged for review** and keeps the lines that were read, so nothing is lost silently.
- The guards that check the model's text against the source now check the *whole* document.

**Results**
- Stress S18 (the 35-page PDF): **105 of 105 lines**, up from 90 plus a review flag. The stress inbox is now **141/141 lines with no extra lines**, and review is right on every email.
- 4 new tests use a fake model, so they're free and offline. They cover the split, no line added twice, nothing taken from the context sections, and a failed window flagging the email.
- All 68 tests pass. Dev replays **byte-identical**, because PDFs of 30 pages or fewer produce exactly the same input as before.
- Live cost of this work: about $0.07.

**Two moments worth remembering for the interview**
1. **The model was more careful than my wording.** On the first live run, it read all the pages but still flagged the email: "pages 31–35 are not visible". It was right to worry, because my note only said those pages "follow". I fixed the cause, and the note now tells it the system reads and merges them. The alternative would have been a code rule that deletes review reasons mentioning pages, which is fragile.
2. **I changed one expected answer, and said so.** S18 was pre-registered as "needs review" because the old design couldn't read past page 30. The design changed, so the expectation changed. I did it before the new run and recorded it in the commit and in the test file.

**Note:** DECISIONS.md is now about 1,360 words, over the two-page limit. I'll trim it in the final docs pass.

**Next: quoting smarts in the matcher.**
- Notice when the customer's unit doesn't match how we sell it, like "12 lengths" of pipe sold per foot.
- For ambiguous lines, suggest the likely part from the rest of the email, but still leave the decision to a person.

Shall I go ahead?
yes

Here's the design before the code. Both features are **advice to the rep, never a silent change**:

**1. Unit check.** The README says quantities are recorded as the customer stated them, never converted. But pipe is sold **per foot**, while customers ask for "12 lengths". So when the customer's unit differs from how the matched part is sold, the reason says so, and does the arithmetic when the length is stated: *"sold per FT: 12 × 21 ft lengths = 252 FT"*. If the length isn't stated: *"sold per FT; length not stated, ask the customer"*. `qty` stays as the customer wrote it.

**2. A suggestion for ambiguous lines, from the rest of the email.** The stress test's zipped BOM is a real example. The gasket came back ambiguous between 150# and 300#, but the flanges on the same request are 300#. A rep would pick the 300# gasket. So for an ambiguous line, the matcher looks at what the email's *matched* lines agree on, for the attributes the candidates differ in. If that leaves exactly one candidate, it's **listed first and named in the reason as likely**. The answer stays `ambiguous` with no SKU, so a person confirms.

content.text:
Here's the design before the code. Both features are **advice to the rep, never a silent change**:

**1. Unit check.** The README says quantities are recorded as the customer stated them, never converted. But pipe is sold **per foot**, while customers ask for "12 lengths". So when the customer's unit differs from how the matched part is sold, the reason says so, and does the arithmetic when the length is stated: *"sold per FT: 12 × 21 ft lengths = 252 FT"*. If the length isn't stated: *"sold per FT; length not stated, ask the customer"*. `qty` stays as the customer wrote it.

**2. A suggestion for ambiguous lines, from the rest of the email.** The stress test's zipped BOM is a real example. The gasket came back ambiguous between 150# and 300#, but the flanges on the same request are 300#. A rep would pick the 300# gasket. So for an ambiguous line, the matcher looks at what the email's *matched* lines agree on, for the attributes the candidates differ in. If that leaves exactly one candidate, it's **listed first and named in the reason as likely**. The answer stays `ambiguous` with no SKU, so a person confirms.

First, let me check whether the official format checker accepts extra fields on a line, which decides whether I add a field or keep everything in the reason:

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# MATCHER

Built: [rfq/matcher.py](rfq/matcher.py). It runs inside `parse` and adds `sku` / `match` /
`match_reason` (and `candidates` when ambiguous) to every line. It is code only: no model calls,
so it costs nothing and the keyless replay produces it too. Tests: [tests/test_matcher.py](tests/test_matcher.py).

## The decision

The costly failure is a **confident wrong part**: the nearest part, one attribute off, quoted
as if it were what the customer asked for. So the matcher only says `matched` when exactly one
stocked part agrees with everything the customer wrote, and it says why in one checkable line.

1. **Normalise the line into the catalog's own columns.** These are product, size, spec (schedule
   or pressure class), material, ends, and stated features (full/std port, LR/SR, wafer, lug,
   inner ring). Sizes: `1 1/2"`, `1.5"` → `1-1/2`; `8" x 6"` → `8 x 6`; bolt thread pitch
   dropped (`5/8"-11` → `5/8`); a length written apart from the diameter is joined
   (`close nipple`, `B7, 4-1/2" long`). Specs: `Class 150`/`150 lb` → `150#`; `Schedule 40`
   → `SCH 40`. Ends: butt weld → BW, NPT/threaded → THD (pipe: TBE / T&C / TOE / PE / BE).
   These are the README's equivalences plus standard trade usage. No dev strings.
2. **Candidates = same product and same size.** If there are none: `not_in_catalog`
   ("no y-strainer stocked in 6\"").
3. **Every attribute the customer stated must agree.** An attribute the customer *didn't*
   state is not a requirement, unless the remaining parts differ on it (step 4).
   - Schedules 40/40S and 80/80S count as equal up to 8" (same wall per ASME B36.19), not above.
   - "A53B" or "black pipe" excludes galvanized.
   - An attribute the catalog doesn't record for that product (rod has no end type) cannot
     disagree.
4. **One part left → `matched`.** It names the part. **None left → `not_in_catalog`.** The reason
   names the nearest stocked part and exactly what's off: "nearest RL-43757 FLG BLIND 4\" 150#
   A105 RF is off: 150# not 300#". A rep checks that in seconds. **Several left → `ambiguous`**,
   with the candidates and the attribute the customer didn't state ("customer did not state
   product": slip-on, weld neck or blind?). That is "ask the customer", never a guess.
5. **A material, grade or end the catalog doesn't carry means `not_in_catalog`, never the nearest
   steel part.** This covers copper, PVC, duplex, 321/347, chrome-moly P11/P22, solder/grooved
   ends, and **any ASTM standard the catalog's materials don't come from** (A350, A694, A333…).
   It is "known standards only", because a list of bad grades is never complete. Without this,
   an A350 LF2 low-temperature flange would "match" the A105 flange: right size, right class,
   wrong metal. A line whose product can't be read is `ambiguous`, never matched.

## Where a model helps, and what it must never decide

**Helps:**
- reading messy descriptions into attributes when the rules find nothing ("FS 90 3M SW" style
  shorthand);
- for an ambiguous line, drafting the question to the customer.

**Never decides:**
- the SKU;
- that a part is "close enough";
- that an unstated attribute can be assumed.

Any model suggestion would go back through steps 2–4, so the model can only *narrow* to a part
that code confirms, never pick one. I didn't add a model step: on dev the rules alone reach
every line, and an unexplained model choice is exactly the confident-wrong risk.

## How it's measured

The scorer (`scripts/score.py`) prints the README's three numbers. Confident wrong comes first.

| | dev (24 emails, 210 lines) |
|---|---|
| confident wrong matches | **0** |
| not-in-catalog recall | **16/16** |
| match accuracy | **210/210** |

**The generated test (`scripts/matcher_fuzz.py`).** This is the check that mattered. Every
catalog part is written as a customer would write it, in random wording and order (WNRF,
class 150, SS316, 2 1/2 inch, 3M…). The expected answers come from the catalog *table*, not the
matcher's logic:
- **fully stated:** must give that SKU;
- **one attribute swapped for one not stocked:** must give not-in-catalog;
- **material left out:** gives whatever the table says is left.

The **first run found 113 confident wrong matches** on the version that scored 210/210 on dev.
- Named grades were too loose: WP316L on a valve matched the F316L valve.
- `A-105 class 150` was read as class 105.
- WNRF/SORF and 3M were unknown.
- My 40S equivalence ran in both directions.

After the fixes: **0 confident wrong in ~19,700 lines over four seeds**. The 40/40S, metal-family
and twin-part policies are written into the generator and documented here. A pytest runs one seed
on every test run. Caveat: the generator's vocabulary is mine, so it tests combinations and order,
not wording neither of us thought of.

Dev is also what I tuned on, so it overstates. The first unseen check was the stress inbox
(118 lines, no SKU key). There I read every decision, and it exposed the copper/A350 gap (step 5).
The tests pin traps that aren't in dev: one attribute off, a stocked-elsewhere grade, an
unstated flange type, the 40S/80S boundary.

In production the real measure is the **rep overturn rate**. The viewer's accept/overturn buttons
write `parsed.rep_decisions.json` next to the system's answer, not over it. Every overturn of a
`matched` line is a confident-wrong to investigate.

**Held-out prediction:** confident wrong **0–2**, not-in-catalog recall **~85%**, match
accuracy **~85%** of paired lines.

## Known weaknesses

- **It reads only our `description`.** If extraction drops the schedule from a line, the matcher
  can't see it. It then says `ambiguous` (safe) or, if only one part exists, `matched` on less
  than the customer wrote.
- **Non-ASTM material names are still a list.** Unknown ASTM numbers are caught generically, but a
  trade name nobody listed ("Hastelloy" is listed; "Alloy 625" is not) is ignored and could
  match a steel part.
- **Unstated trims and features are accepted.** A gate valve "800# A105 SW" matches the
  13CR-trim part, because that is the only one stocked. A rep may want that confirmed.

"""Check the submission the way the graders will, from a fresh clone of the last commit.

    python scripts/verify.py [--keep]

1. clone HEAD into a temp folder (uncommitted changes are not in the submission: warned)
2. parse dev with OPENAI_API_KEY removed -> must equal the committed parsed.json byte for byte
3. parse again -> must make 0 new model calls (idempotent)
4. data/check_format.py on the output
5. score dev and stress: 0 silent losses, 0 hallucinated lines, 0 confident wrong matches
6. the test suite, and one seed of the generated matcher test
7. hygiene: nothing key-shaped in any tracked file (ai-sessions/ included), repo under 50 MB

Exit code 0 only if every check passes. Uses this interpreter's installed packages.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
PY = sys.executable
KEY = re.compile(rb"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])sk-(?!REDACTED)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{20,}")

results: list[tuple[str, bool, str]] = []


def check(name: str, ok: bool, detail: str = "") -> bool:
    results.append((name, ok, detail))
    print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {name}" + (f"  ({detail})" if detail else ""), flush=True)
    return ok


def run(args: list[str], cwd: Path, env: dict | None = None) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    return subprocess.run(args, cwd=cwd, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")


def metric(out: str, label: str) -> str:
    m = re.search(rf"^{re.escape(label)}\s+(.+)$", out, re.M)
    return m[1].strip() if m else "?"


def main() -> int:
    keep = "--keep" in sys.argv
    dirty = run(["git", "status", "--porcelain", "--untracked-files=no"], ROOT).stdout.strip()
    head = run(["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"], ROOT).stdout.strip()
    print(f"verifying commit {head}" + ("  (WARNING: uncommitted changes are not checked)" if dirty else ""))

    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="rfq-verify-"))
    clone = tmp / "repo"
    try:
        c = run(["git", "clone", "-q", str(ROOT), str(clone)], tmp)
        if not check("fresh clone of HEAD", c.returncode == 0, c.stderr.strip()[:200]):
            return 1
        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if k not in ("OPENAI_API_KEY", "RFQ_MODEL", "RFQ_EFFORT")}
        env["PYTHONIOENCODING"] = "utf-8"
        if (clone / ".env").exists():  # git-ignored; never in a clone, but be sure
            (clone / ".env").unlink()

        # 2-3. keyless replay, twice
        for n in (1, 2):
            r = run([PY, "-m", "rfq", "parse", "--emails", "data/dev/emails", "--out", f"out{n}.json"], clone, env)
            if not check(f"parse dev without a key (run {n})", r.returncode == 0, r.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1][:150] if r.stderr.strip() else ""):
                return 1
        same = (clone / "out1.json").read_bytes() == (ROOT / "parsed.json").read_bytes()
        check("keyless output == committed parsed.json (byte for byte)", same)
        rep = json.loads((clone / "out2.report.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["totals"]
        check("second run makes no new model calls", rep["model_calls"] == 0 and rep["fallbacks"] == 0,
              f"calls {rep['model_calls']}, fallbacks {rep['fallbacks']}, cache hits {rep['cache_hits']}/{rep['emails']}")
        check("cost reported per email", rep.get("avg_cost_usd_per_email", 0) > 0,
              f"${rep.get('avg_cost_usd_per_email')}/email, ${rep.get('cost_usd_if_uncached')} per dev inbox uncached")

        # 4. format
        f = run([PY, "data/check_format.py", "out1.json", "--emails", "data/dev/emails"], clone, env)
        check("check_format.py", f.returncode == 0, (f.stdout + f.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1][:120])

        # 5. scores
        for label, parsed, key, cache in (("dev", "out1.json", "data/dev/answer_key.json", None),
                                          ("stress", "st.json", "tests/stress/answer_key.json", "tests/stress/cache")):
            if cache:
                run([PY, "-m", "rfq", "parse", "--emails", "tests/stress/emails", "--cache", cache, "--out", parsed], clone, env)
            s = run([PY, "scripts/score.py", parsed, key], clone, env).stdout
            silent, halluc = metric(s, "silent losses"), metric(s, "hallucinated lines")
            wrong = re.search(r"confident wrong (\d+)", s)
            check(f"{label}: 0 silent losses, 0 hallucinated lines", silent == "0" and halluc == "0",
                  f"classes {metric(s, 'classification')}; recall {metric(s, 'line recall')}; "
                  f"precision {metric(s, 'line precision')}; context {metric(s, 'context carried')}")
            if wrong:
                check(f"{label}: 0 confident wrong catalog matches", wrong[1] == "0",
                      re.search(r"matcher: .+", s)[0].replace("matcher: ", ""))

        # 6. tests
        t = run([PY, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"], clone, env)
        check("test suite", t.returncode == 0, (t.stdout.strip().splitlines() or ["?"])[-1])
        z = run([PY, "scripts/matcher_fuzz.py", "--seed", "101"], clone, env).stdout
        check("generated matcher test (seed 101)", "confident wrong matches: 0" in z,
              (z.splitlines() or ["?"])[0])

        # 7. hygiene
        files = run(["git", "ls-files", "-z"], clone).stdout.split("\0")
        leaks = [p for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file() and KEY.search((clone / p).read_bytes())]
        check("no API key in any tracked file", not leaks, ", ".join(leaks[:5]))
        size = sum((clone / p).stat().st_size for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file())
        git_size = sum(f.stat().st_size for f in (clone / ".git").rglob("*") if f.is_file())
        check("repo under 50 MB", size + git_size < 50 * 1024 * 1024,
              f"{(size + git_size) / 1e6:.1f} MB incl. history")
    finally:
        if keep:
            print(f"clone kept at {clone}")
        else:
            shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)

    failed = [n for n, ok, _ in results if not ok]
    print(f"\n{len(results) - len(failed)}/{len(results)} checks passed" + (f"; FAILED: {', '.join(failed)}" if failed else ""))
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

        check("check_format.py", f.returncode == 0, (f.stdout + f.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1][:120])

        # 5. scores
        for label, parsed, key, cache in (("dev", "out1.json", "data/dev/answer_key.json", None),
                                          ("stress", "st.json", "tests/stress/answer_key.json", "tests/stress/cache")):
            if cache:
                run([PY, "-m", "rfq", "parse", "--emails", "tests/stress/emails", "--cache", cache, "--out", parsed], clone, env)
            s = run([PY, "scripts/score.py", parsed, key], clone, env).stdout
            silent, halluc = metric(s, "silent losses"), metric(s, "hallucinated lines")
            wrong = re.search(r"confident wrong (\d+)", s)
            check(f"{label}: 0 silent losses, 0 hallucinated lines", silent == "0" and halluc == "0",
                  f"classes {metric(s, 'classification')}; recall {metric(s, 'line recall')}; "
                  f"precision {metric(s, 'line precision')}; context {metric(s, 'context carried')}")
            if wrong:
                check(f"{label}: 0 confident wrong catalog matches", wrong[1] == "0",
                      re.search(r"matcher: .+", s)[0].replace("matcher: ", ""))

        # 6. tests
        t = run([PY, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"], clone, env)
        check("test suite", t.returncode == 0, (t.stdout.strip().splitlines() or ["?"])[-1])
        z = run([PY, "scripts/matcher_fuzz.py", "--seed", "101"], clone, env).stdout
        check("generated matcher test (seed 101)", "confident wrong matches: 0" in z,
              (z.splitlines() or ["?"])[0])

        # 7. hygiene
        files = run(["git", "ls-files", "-z"], clone).stdout.split("\0")
        leaks = [p for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file() and KEY.search((clone / p).read_bytes())]
        check("no API key in any tracked file", not leaks, ", ".join(leaks[:5]))
        size = sum((clone / p).stat().st_size for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file())
        git_size = sum(f.stat().st_size for f in (clone / ".git").rglob("*") if f.is_file())
        check("repo under 50 MB", size + git_size < 50 * 1024 * 1024,
              f"{(size + git_size) / 1e6:.1f} MB incl. history")
    finally:
        if keep:
            print(f"clone kept at {clone}")
        else:
            shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)

    failed = [n for n, ok, _ in results if not ok]
    print(f"\n{len(results) - len(failed)}/{len(results)} checks passed" + (f"; FAILED: {', '.join(failed)}" if failed else ""))
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

The plan for `scripts/verify.py`. It checks the **committed** state, not my working folder, because that's what graders get:

1. **Fresh clone** of the latest commit into a temp folder. It warns if there are uncommitted changes, since those wouldn't be in the submission.
2. **No-key replay:** run `parse` on dev with the API key removed, and compare byte-for-byte with the committed `parsed.json`.
3. **Idempotence:** run it again and confirm zero new model calls.
4. **Format check** with the assignment's own `check_format.py`.
5. **Scores** on dev and stress, failing on any silent loss, hallucinated line or confident wrong match.
6. **Tests**, plus one seed of the big matcher test.
7. **Submission hygiene:** no API key anywhere in tracked files (including `ai-sessions/`), and repo size under the brief's 50 MB.

"""Check the submission the way the graders will, from a fresh clone of the last commit.

    python scripts/verify.py [--keep]

1. clone HEAD into a temp folder (uncommitted changes are not in the submission: warned)
2. parse dev with OPENAI_API_KEY removed -> must equal the committed parsed.json byte for byte
3. parse again -> must make 0 new model calls (idempotent)
4. data/check_format.py on the output
5. score dev and stress: 0 silent losses, 0 hallucinated lines, 0 confident wrong matches
6. the test suite, and one seed of the generated matcher test
7. hygiene: nothing key-shaped in any tracked file (ai-sessions/ included), repo under 50 MB

Exit code 0 only if every check passes. Uses this interpreter's installed packages.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
PY = sys.executable
KEY = re.compile(rb"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])sk-(?!REDACTED)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{20,}")

results: list[tuple[str, bool, str]] = []


def check(name: str, ok: bool, detail: str = "") -> bool:
    results.append((name, ok, detail))
    print(f"  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {name}" + (f"  ({detail})" if detail else ""), flush=True)
    return ok


def run(args: list[str], cwd: Path, env: dict | None = None) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    return subprocess.run(args, cwd=cwd, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")


def metric(out: str, label: str) -> str:
    m = re.search(rf"^{re.escape(label)}\s+(.+)$", out, re.M)
    return m[1].strip() if m else "?"


def main() -> int:
    keep = "--keep" in sys.argv
    dirty = run(["git", "status", "--porcelain", "--untracked-files=no"], ROOT).stdout.strip()
    head = run(["git", "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"], ROOT).stdout.strip()
    print(f"verifying commit {head}" + ("  (WARNING: uncommitted changes are not checked)" if dirty else ""))

    tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="rfq-verify-"))
    clone = tmp / "repo"
    try:
        c = run(["git", "clone", "-q", str(ROOT), str(clone)], tmp)
        if not check("fresh clone of HEAD", c.returncode == 0, c.stderr.strip()[:200]):
            return 1
        env = {k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if k not in ("OPENAI_API_KEY", "RFQ_MODEL", "RFQ_EFFORT")}
        env["PYTHONIOENCODING"] = "utf-8"
        if (clone / ".env").exists():  # git-ignored; never in a clone, but be sure
            (clone / ".env").unlink()

        # 2-3. keyless replay, twice
        for n in (1, 2):
            r = run([PY, "-m", "rfq", "parse", "--emails", "data/dev/emails", "--out", f"out{n}.json"], clone, env)
            if not check(f"parse dev without a key (run {n})", r.returncode == 0, r.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1][:150] if r.stderr.strip() else ""):
                return 1
        same = (clone / "out1.json").read_bytes() == (ROOT / "parsed.json").read_bytes()
        check("keyless output == committed parsed.json (byte for byte)", same)
        rep = json.loads((clone / "out2.report.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["totals"]
        check("second run makes no new model calls", rep["model_calls"] == 0 and rep["fallbacks"] == 0,
              f"calls {rep['model_calls']}, fallbacks {rep['fallbacks']}, cache hits {rep['cache_hits']}/{rep['emails']}")
        check("cost reported per email", rep.get("avg_cost_usd_per_email", 0) > 0,
              f"${rep.get('avg_cost_usd_per_email')}/email, ${rep.get('cost_usd_if_uncached')} per dev inbox uncached")

        # 4. format
        f = run([PY, "data/check_format.py", "out1.json", "--emails", "data/dev/emails"], clone, env)
        check("check_format.py", f.returncode == 0, (f.stdout + f.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1][:120])

        # 5. scores
        for label, parsed, key, cache in (("dev", "out1.json", "data/dev/answer_key.json", None),
                                          ("stress", "st.json", "tests/stress/answer_key.json", "tests/stress/cache")):
            if cache:
                run([PY, "-m", "rfq", "parse", "--emails", "tests/stress/emails", "--cache", cache, "--out", parsed], clone, env)
            s = run([PY, "scripts/score.py", parsed, key], clone, env).stdout
            silent, halluc = metric(s, "silent losses"), metric(s, "hallucinated lines")
            wrong = re.search(r"confident wrong (\d+)", s)
            check(f"{label}: 0 silent losses, 0 hallucinated lines", silent == "0" and halluc == "0",
                  f"classes {metric(s, 'classification')}; recall {metric(s, 'line recall')}; "
                  f"precision {metric(s, 'line precision')}; context {metric(s, 'context carried')}")
            if wrong:
                check(f"{label}: 0 confident wrong catalog matches", wrong[1] == "0",
                      re.search(r"matcher: .+", s)[0].replace("matcher: ", ""))

        # 6. tests
        t = run([PY, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"], clone, env)
        check("test suite", t.returncode == 0, (t.stdout.strip().splitlines() or ["?"])[-1])
        z = run([PY, "scripts/matcher_fuzz.py", "--seed", "101"], clone, env).stdout
        check("generated matcher test (seed 101)", "confident wrong matches: 0" in z,
              (z.splitlines() or ["?"])[0])

        # 7. hygiene
        files = run(["git", "ls-files", "-z"], clone).stdout.split("\0")
        leaks = [p for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file() and KEY.search((clone / p).read_bytes())]
        check("no API key in any tracked file", not leaks, ", ".join(leaks[:5]))
        size = sum((clone / p).stat().st_size for p in files if p and (clone / p).is_file())
        git_size = sum(f.stat().st_size for f in (clone / ".git").rglob("*") if f.is_file())
        check("repo under 50 MB", size + git_size < 50 * 1024 * 1024,
              f"{(size + git_size) / 1e6:.1f} MB incl. history")
    finally:
        if keep:
            print(f"clone kept at {clone}")
        else:
            shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)

    failed = [n for n, ok, _ in results if not ok]
    print(f"\n{len(results) - len(failed)}/{len(results)} checks passed" + (f"; FAILED: {', '.join(failed)}" if failed else ""))
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# RUNNING

Windows, native Python 3.11+ (developed and tested on 3.12.10). No Docker needed.

## Setup (one step, from a fresh clone or unzip)

```powershell
python -m venv .venv; .venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

(macOS/Linux/WSL: `python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`)

## Run

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq parse --emails data\dev\emails --out parsed.json
```

- **With a key:** set `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the environment (or put `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` in a
  git-ignored `.env` in the repo root). New emails call the model; every answer is saved to
  `cache\`.
- **Without a key:** answers are replayed from `cache\`. On dev this reproduces the committed
  `parsed.json` byte for byte, with zero calls (checked from a fresh clone). An email with no
  cached answer is not dropped: it is classified from its headers and flagged `needs_review`.
- **A second run** on the same inbox makes no new model calls (the cache key is a sha256 of the
  model, effort, prompt and the email's full content).
- Every run also writes `parsed.report.json`: per-email calls, tokens, cost, cache hits,
  warnings and the model's one-line reason for its classification, plus totals.

Format check: `.venv\Scripts\python data\check_format.py parsed.json --emails data\dev\emails`
(24 emails, 0 problems).

## Model

`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17` (a pinned snapshot, so a re-run can't drift), reasoning effort
`medium`, OpenAI Responses API with a strict JSON schema. One call per email, plus at most one
retry when code finds a numbered table row that no extracted line covers (1 of 24 dev emails).
Override with `--model` / `--effort` or `RFQ_MODEL` / `RFQ_EFFORT`. Other options: `--offline`
(never call the model), `--workers N` (default 4), `--cache DIR`.

**Catalog matching** (the optional matcher, [MATCHER.md](MATCHER.md)) runs inside `parse` against
`data\catalog.csv` and adds `sku` / `match` / `match_reason` to every line. It is code only:
no model calls, $0, and the keyless replay includes it. `--catalog FILE` to point elsewhere,
`--no-match` to skip.

## Cost (dev inbox, 24 emails, from `parsed.report.json`)

| | |
|---|---|
| model calls | 25 (24 + 1 coverage retry) |
| tokens per email | ~3,940 on average (input + output, incl. reasoning) |
| cost per email | **$0.0072** average |
| full inbox, uncached | **$0.17** |
| re-run / replay | $0.00 |
| latency per call | median 4.9 s, worst 24 s |

Prices used ($ per 1M tokens, `rfq/llm.py`): input 0.75, cached input 0.075, output 4.50.

## Other tools

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\score.py parsed.json data\dev\answer_key.json      # score vs the key
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq.viewer --emails data\dev\emails --parsed parsed.json --key data\dev\answer_key.json
                                                                   # local web view, one email end to end
.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt; .venv\Scripts\python -m pytest -q   # 68 tests
.venv\Scripts\python -m rfq parse --emails tests\stress\emails --cache tests\stress\cache --out tests\stress\parsed.json
.venv\Scripts\python scripts\score.py tests\stress\parsed.json tests\stress\answer_key.json   # stress inbox (22 emails)
```

The viewer listens on `localhost:8765` and makes no outbound calls. Its only write is a rep's
accept/overturn of a catalog match, saved to `parsed.rep_decisions.json` (git-ignored), never
into `parsed.json`.

11	- **Code reads the files.** Every part becomes text or images before the model sees it: xlsx with
12	  sheet state, merged cells, hidden rows and struck cells marked; docx in document order with
13	  tracked deletions removed; PDF rows rebuilt from word positions, scans rendered to images;
14	  HTML tables flattened with `~~strike~~` kept. A broken part becomes `kind=unreadable` with a
15	  note — it never raises.
16	- **The model judges.** Classification, which lines are requests, and the self-contained
17	  description (heading scope, overrides beating defaults, quoted history is not a request).
18	  The prompt states principles, not dev strings; its one worked example is invented.
19	- **Code checks anything that is a fact.** Struck and hidden-only lines are dropped whatever the
20	  model said; non-request classes carry no lines; a request with zero lines, an unreadable part
21	  or a truncated document is always `needs_review`; `source` must be a real part; `raw` is
22	  snapped to the unique matching source row (the model's copy of a row varies run to run, and
23	  graders pair on `raw`). If a numbered table row is accounted for by no line, the model is
24	  asked once more with that row named (caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, $0.004).
25	- **Code links threads.** `revises` from In-Reply-To/References, then subject + sender domain;
26	  `duplicate_of` needs the same sender, ≤30 days, identical attachment hashes and matching lines.
27	
28	**Measured, not guessed.** I wrote a scorer that implements the README's grading, and a
29	22-email stress inbox (`tests/stress/`) for situations dev doesn't show — tracked changes, a
30	Spanish request, a rotated photo, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a
31	byte-identical second delivery, a 35-page PDF, a BOM inside a zip, an iPhone HEIC photo. Its
32	answers were written **before** running the system. Dev: 24/24 classes, 210/210 lines,
33	0 silent / 0 hallucinated, context 172/173. Stress: 22/22 classes, 141/141 lines,
34	0 hallucinated, context 140/141. Format tests generate what neither inbox has: zip bombs,
35	password zips, misnamed .xlsx, legacy .xls, sideways phone photos. Legacy .doc/.msg are
36	flagged rather than read, because I couldn't test a reader for them.
37	**Rejected:** gpt-5.5 — 4.6× the cost and *worse* on context (it "corrected" `A53B` to
38	`A53 Grade B`); a two-call classify-then-extract design — twice the cost, and the classifier
39	needs the same reading anyway.
40	
41	## Something in the data that surprised you
42	
43	The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request. E013's bounce carries a
44	perfect numbered list of valves with quantities — it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier. E011 is a
45	supplier's price list. E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)` with the
46	superseded rows; a reader that loads every sheet quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the
47	filename calls it a revision although no earlier email exists. Meanwhile the real requests hide:
48	the spec is in a merged cell two rows above (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB UNLESS NOTED`) with
49	one row overriding it to SCH 80, or on a phone photo of a nameplate. So most of the accuracy came
50	from *ingest* — marking hidden, struck and merged structure faithfully — not from the prompt.
51	
52	## Something in the brief or README you disagree with
53	
54	The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
55	brief's own costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
56	person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
57	quote, an out-of-office from the buyer on a job with a deadline. Under the contract those come back
58	`auto_reply` / `other` with nothing to act on. **What I did:** kept the contract in
59	`parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because the grader scores it), and made the model state a
60	one-line reason for every classification; it is in `parsed.report.json` and the viewer, so a
61	person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate `attention`
62	field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.
63	
64	## Predicted held-out numbers, and two kinds of email I expect to get wrong
65	
66	Dev is 100% partly because I looked at it; the stress inbox (unseen until written) is the fairer
67	guide. For ~40 held-out emails: **silent losses 0** (every request with no lines is flagged by
68	code), **hallucinated lines 2–5**, **lost/phantom 1–2**, classification **~90%**, line recall
69	**~90%**, precision **~95%**, qty **~95%**, uom/source **~97%**, context carried **~85%**,
70	links mostly right, needs_review P/R **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt).
71	
72	1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The reading is all we have, so a misread `6`/`8`,
73	   a missed line or a `raw` that pairs badly with the key's reading costs qty and recall. Code
74	   cannot check a picture; only the review flag helps, and the model flags too rarely.
75	2. **Terse revisions against an earlier email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the
76	   original list; when it's only partly quoted, the "complete order as now intended" will be
77	   incomplete or wrong. A second hazard on the same boundary: Rev B / resend / "also add" as new
78	   rfq vs revision — I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*", which held-out
79	   may draw differently.
80	
81	## How this runs for real
82	
83	**Built today:** content-addressed cache (sha256 of model + effort + prompt + full content incl.
84	image bytes, atomic writes), 3 retries with timeout, a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive
85	failures, a per-email header fallback, windowed reading of long PDFs, per-email isolation, and a per-email
86	cost/token report. **Not built:** the webhook, a queue, a database.
87	
88	- **3,000 emails a day.** Measured cost is $0.0072 per email (3,940 tokens incl. reasoning) →
89	  about **$22/day**. Median latency 4.9 s, worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 per minute, so one worker
90	  keeps up. Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run
91	  `process_one`; thread linking moves from "whole inbox" to a lookup in a store of past emails by
92	  Message-ID, subject and domain.
93	- **Provider down for two hours.** Today: retries, then the breaker trips and every remaining
94	  email gets the fallback — headers decide auto_reply/bulk, everything else becomes
95	  `rfq` + `needs_review` ("not read automatically"). Fallbacks are not cached, so the next run
96	  calls the model for exactly those emails. For real I'd hold them in the queue with backoff
97	  for a while before handing them to people, with an alert — 250 emails to a person is worse
98	  than a 2-hour delay.
99	- **A 300-page PDF.** Built: it is read in windows of 30 pages (or 16 scanned pages), one cached
100	  call each, about 10 calls and roughly $0.30.
101	  - Each window also sees the document's first page and the end of the previous window as
102	    context-only, because a heading on page 2 can govern rows on page 40.
103	  - A window that fails flags the email for review and keeps the lines that were read.
104	  - Above 300 pages the rest is flagged.
105	  - Stress S18 (35 pages): all 105 rows, where the 30-page cap lost 15.
106	
107	  Not done: a 300-page spec book is often not a list at all; a page-relevance pass first
108	  would save most of those calls.
109	- **The same email delivered twice.** Built two ways: the second delivery hashes to the same
110	  cache key, so it costs nothing, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` the first
111	  (stress S13 is a byte copy). For real, dedupe on Message-ID + body hash at the webhook before
112	  any work.
113	
114	## Known broken / next
115	
116	- `raw` for pictures varies between runs (E023's nameplate); the cache makes it stable for
117	  replay, not right.
118	- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
119	- The matcher reads only our `description`, so a context miss in extraction becomes a matching
120	  miss (MATCHER.md lists its own weaknesses).
121	- Next: page-window chunking, an `attention` field, and using the viewer's rep overturns of
122	  matches as the matcher's running error rate.

# DECISIONS

**Time spent:** about 5 hours.

## Who decides what

`ingest` (code) → **one model call per email** (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, effort medium, strict
JSON schema) → `guards` (code) → `threads` (code) → `matcher` (code; see [MATCHER.md](MATCHER.md)).

- **Code reads the files**, keeping the structure that carries meaning: hidden sheets and rows,
  merged headings and struck cells (xlsx/xls); tracked deletions (docx); PDF rows rebuilt from
  word positions, scans sent as images; zips unpacked; photos turned upright. A broken part
  becomes `unreadable` with a reason. It never raises.
- **The model judges.** It decides the class, which lines are requests, and the self-contained
  description (heading scope, overrides beat defaults, quoted history is not a request). The prompt
  states principles; its one example is invented, not a dev row.
- **Code checks every fact it can.**
  - Struck and hidden-only lines are dropped, whatever the model said.
  - Non-requests carry no lines.
  - A request with no lines, or an unreadable part, is always `needs_review`.
  - `source` must be a real part.
  - `raw` is snapped to the unique matching source row, because the model's copy of a row varies
    run to run and grading pairs on `raw`.
  - A numbered row that no line accounts for gets one more model call with that row named. This
    caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, for $0.004.

**Measured, not guessed.** I wrote a scorer implementing the README's grading, and a 22-email
**stress inbox** of situations dev lacks, with answers written **before** each run: tracked
changes, Spanish, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a byte-identical
redelivery, a 35-page PDF, a BOM in a zip, an iPhone HEIC photo.

| | classes | lines (recall/precision) | silent | hallucinated | context |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dev | 24/24 | 210/210 · 210/210 | 0 | 0 | 172/173 |
| stress | 22/22 | 141/141 · 141/141 | 0 | 0 | 140/141 |

`scripts/verify.py` re-checks all of this, the keyless replay and the hygiene rules from a fresh
clone in about 15 s.

**Rejected:**
- gpt-5.5: 4.6× the cost and *worse* on context (it "corrected" `A53B` to `A53 Grade B`).
- Classify-then-extract in two calls: double the cost for the same reading.
- Readers for `.doc`/`.msg`: I couldn't test them here, so they're flagged instead.

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request.
- E013's bounce carries a perfect numbered list of valves: it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier.
- E011 is a supplier's price list.
- E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)`. A reader that loads every sheet
  quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the filename calls it a revision with no earlier
  email.

Meanwhile the real requests hide: in a merged cell two rows up (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB
UNLESS NOTED`, with one row overriding it to SCH 80), or on a photo of a nameplate. Most of the
accuracy came from *ingest* faithfully marking hidden, struck and merged structure, not from the
prompt.

A second surprise: **dev agrees with you too easily.** The matcher scored 210/210 on dev. A test
generated from the catalog, whose expected answers come from the catalog table and not from my
logic, then found **113 confident wrong matches**: grades matched too loosely, `A-105 class 150`
read as class 105.

## Something in the brief or README you disagree with

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, a buyer's out-of-office on a deadline job. Under the contract these come back `auto_reply`
/ `other` with nothing to act on.

**What I did:** kept the contract in `parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because it is scored). The
model also states a one-line reason for every classification, shown in `parsed.report.json` and
the viewer, so a person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate
`attention` field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 100% partly because I looked at it; stress is the fairer guide. For ~40 held-out emails:

| metric | prediction |
|---|---|
| silent losses | **0** (code flags any request with no lines) |
| hallucinated lines | **2–5** |
| lost / phantom | **1–2** |
| classification | **~90%** |
| line recall / precision | **~90% / ~95%** |
| qty | **~95%** |
| uom / source | **~97%** |
| context carried | **~85%** |
| needs_review P / R | **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt) |
| matcher: confident wrong | **0–2** |
| matcher: not-in-catalog recall | **~85%** |

1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The model's reading is all there is. A misread
   `6`/`8`, a missed line or a `raw` that pairs badly costs qty and recall. Code can't check a
   picture, and the model flags too rarely.
2. **Terse revisions of an email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the original list,
   so the "complete order as now intended" will be incomplete. The same boundary, Rev B / resend
   / "also add", is new rfq or revision? I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*";
   held-out may draw it differently.

## How this runs for real

**Built:**
- a content-addressed cache (sha256 of model, effort, prompt and full content incl. image bytes;
  atomic writes);
- 3 retries with timeouts and a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive failures;
- a header-based fallback per email, and per-email isolation;
- windowed long PDFs;
- a per-email cost and token report.

**Not built:** the webhook, a queue, a database.

- **3,000 emails a day.** $0.0072 per email measured (about 3,940 tokens), so about **$22/day**.
  Median latency is 4.9 s and the worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 a minute, so one worker keeps up.
  Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run `process_one`;
  thread linking becomes a lookup in a store of past emails by Message-ID, subject and domain.
- **Provider down for two hours.** Retries, then the breaker trips. The rest get the fallback:
  headers decide auto_reply/bulk, everything else becomes `rfq` + `needs_review`. Fallbacks
  aren't cached, so the next run calls the model for exactly those. For real I'd hold them in the
  queue with backoff and an alert: 250 emails dumped on a person is worse than a 2-hour delay.
- **A 300-page PDF.** Built. It's read in windows of 30 pages (16 if scanned), one cached call
  each: ~10 calls, ~$0.30. Each window also gets page 1 and the previous window's end as
  context-only, because a heading on page 2 can govern page 40. A failed window flags review
  and keeps what was read; past 300 pages the rest is flagged. Stress S18: 105/105 rows (the
  old 30-page cap lost 15). Not done: a relevance pass to skip spec-book pages that hold no
  items.
- **The same email delivered twice.** Built two ways. The redelivery hashes to the same cache
  key, so it's free, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` (stress S13 is a byte copy).
  For real, dedupe on Message-ID plus body hash at the webhook.

## Known broken / next

- `raw` read from pictures varies between runs (E023). The cache makes it stable, not right.
- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
- The matcher reads only our `description`, so a context miss upstream becomes a match miss.
- Next: the `attention` field, and the viewer's rep overturns as the matcher's live error rate.

| qty | **~95%** |
| uom / source | **~97%** |
| context carried | **~85%** |

- windowed long PDFs;

# DECISIONS

**Time spent:** about 5 hours.

## Who decides what

`ingest` (code) → **one model call per email** (`gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`, effort medium, strict
JSON schema) → `guards` (code) → `threads` (code) → `matcher` (code; see [MATCHER.md](MATCHER.md)).

- **Code reads the files**, keeping the structure that carries meaning: hidden sheets and rows,
  merged headings and struck cells (xlsx/xls); tracked deletions (docx); PDF rows rebuilt from
  word positions, scans sent as images; zips unpacked; photos turned upright. A broken part
  becomes `unreadable` with a reason. It never raises.
- **The model judges.** It decides the class, which lines are requests, and the self-contained
  description (heading scope, overrides beat defaults, quoted history is not a request). The prompt
  states principles; its one example is invented, not a dev row.
- **Code checks every fact it can.**
  - Struck and hidden-only lines are dropped, whatever the model said.
  - Non-requests carry no lines.
  - A request with no lines, or an unreadable part, is always `needs_review`.
  - `source` must be a real part.
  - `raw` is snapped to the unique matching source row, because the model's copy of a row varies
    run to run and grading pairs on `raw`.
  - A numbered row that no line accounts for gets one more model call with that row named. This
    caught a silently dropped PO line in E015, for $0.004.

**Measured, not guessed.** I wrote a scorer implementing the README's grading, and a 22-email
**stress inbox** of situations dev lacks, with answers written **before** each run: tracked
changes, Spanish, an invoice with item lines, "make #3 twelve and kill #5", a byte-identical
redelivery, a 35-page PDF, a BOM in a zip, an iPhone HEIC photo.

| | classes | lines (recall/precision) | silent | hallucinated | context |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dev | 24/24 | 210/210 · 210/210 | 0 | 0 | 172/173 |
| stress | 22/22 | 141/141 · 141/141 | 0 | 0 | 140/141 |

`scripts/verify.py` re-checks all of this, the keyless replay and the hygiene rules from a fresh
clone in about 15 s.

**Rejected:** gpt-5.5 (4.6× the cost, *worse* context: it "corrected" `A53B` to `A53 Grade B`);
two calls per email (double cost, same reading); `.doc`/`.msg` readers (untestable here, so
flagged instead).

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request.
- E013's bounce carries a perfect numbered list of valves: it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier.
- E011 is a supplier's price list.
- E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)`. A reader that loads every sheet
  quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the filename calls it a revision with no earlier
  email.

Meanwhile the real requests hide: in a merged cell two rows up (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB
UNLESS NOTED`, with one row overriding it to SCH 80), or on a photo of a nameplate. Most of the
accuracy came from *ingest* faithfully marking hidden, struck and merged structure, not from the
prompt.

A second surprise: **dev agrees with you too easily.** The matcher scored 210/210 on dev. A test
generated from the catalog, whose expected answers come from the catalog table and not from my
logic, then found **113 confident wrong matches**: grades matched too loosely, `A-105 class 150`
read as class 105.

## Something in the brief or README you disagree with

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, a buyer's out-of-office on a deadline job. Under the contract these come back `auto_reply`
/ `other` with nothing to act on.

**What I did:** kept the contract in `parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because it is scored). The
model also states a one-line reason for every classification, shown in `parsed.report.json` and
the viewer, so a person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate
`attention` field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

|---|---|
| silent losses | **0** (code flags any request with no lines) |
| hallucinated lines | **2–5** |
| lost / phantom | **1–2** |
| classification | **~90%** |
| line recall / precision | **~90% / ~95%** |
| qty | **~95%** |
| uom / source | **~97%** |
| context carried | **~85%** |
| needs_review P / R | **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt) |
| matcher: confident wrong | **0–2** |
| matcher: not-in-catalog recall | **~85%** |

2. **Terse revisions of an email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the original list,

two calls per email (double cost, same reading); `.doc`/`.msg` readers (untestable here, so
flagged instead).

## Something in the data that surprised you

The most request-shaped text in the inbox is usually not a request.
- E013's bounce carries a perfect numbered list of valves: it is *our own* RFQ to a supplier.
- E011 is a supplier's price list.
- E005's workbook is named `RevB` and hides a sheet `Rev A (old)`. A reader that loads every sheet
  quotes both revisions, and a model that sees the filename calls it a revision with no earlier
  email.

Meanwhile the real requests hide: in a merged cell two rows up (`ALL FITTINGS BW SCH 40 A234 WPB
UNLESS NOTED`, with one row overriding it to SCH 80), or on a photo of a nameplate. Most of the
accuracy came from *ingest* faithfully marking hidden, struck and merged structure, not from the
prompt.

A second surprise: **dev agrees with you too easily.** The matcher scored 210/210 on dev. A test
generated from the catalog, whose expected answers come from the catalog table and not from my
logic, then found **113 confident wrong matches**: grades matched too loosely, `A-105 class 150`
read as class 105.

## Something in the brief or README you disagree with

The README allows `needs_review` only on `rfq`, `rfq_revision` and `purchase_order`. But the
brief's costliest failure is "a customer who never hears back", and some non-requests need a
person: a bounce of *our quote to a customer*, a "we went with someone else" that should close a
quote, a buyer's out-of-office on a deadline job. Under the contract these come back `auto_reply`
/ `other` with nothing to act on.

**What I did:** kept the contract in `parsed.json` (guards enforce it, because it is scored). The
model also states a one-line reason for every classification, shown in `parsed.report.json` and
the viewer, so a person can see *why* something was set aside. In production I'd add a separate
`attention` field rather than overload `needs_review`. Not built.

## Predicted held-out numbers, and two kinds of email I expect to get wrong

Dev is 100% partly because I looked at it; stress is the fairer guide. For ~40 held-out emails:

| metric | prediction |
|---|---|
| silent losses | **0** (code flags any request with no lines) |
| hallucinated lines | **2–5** |
| lost / phantom | **1–2** |
| classification | **~90%** |
| line recall / precision | **~90% / ~95%** |
| qty | **~95%** |
| uom / source | **~97%** |
| context carried | **~85%** |
| needs_review P / R | **~80% / ~90%** (I flag on doubt) |
| matcher: confident wrong | **0–2** |
| matcher: not-in-catalog recall | **~85%** |

1. **Photos and scans of handwritten lists.** The model's reading is all there is. A misread
   `6`/`8`, a missed line or a `raw` that pairs badly costs qty and recall. Code can't check a
   picture, and the model flags too rarely.
2. **Terse revisions of an email that isn't in the inbox.** "Kill #5" needs the original list,
   so the "complete order as now intended" will be incomplete. The same boundary, Rev B / resend
   / "also add", is new rfq or revision? I chose "revision only if it changes an *earlier email*";
   held-out may draw it differently.

## How this runs for real

**Built:**
- a content-addressed cache (sha256 of model, effort, prompt and full content incl. image bytes;
  atomic writes);
- 3 retries with timeouts and a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive failures;
- a header-based fallback per email, and per-email isolation;
- windowed long PDFs;
- a per-email cost and token report.

**Not built:** the webhook, a queue, a database.

- **3,000 emails a day.** $0.0072 per email measured (about 3,940 tokens), so about **$22/day**.
  Median latency is 4.9 s and the worst 24 s; 3,000/day is ~2 a minute, so one worker keeps up.
  Design: the webhook stores the raw `.eml` and enqueues its hash; workers run `process_one`;
  thread linking becomes a lookup in a store of past emails by Message-ID, subject and domain.
- **Provider down for two hours.** After the retries, the breaker trips and the rest get the
  fallback: auto_reply/bulk by header, everything else `rfq` + `needs_review`. Fallbacks aren't
  cached, so the next run re-calls exactly those. For real: hold them in the queue with backoff
  and an alert. 250 emails on a person's desk is worse than a 2-hour delay.
- **A 300-page PDF.** Built. It's read in windows of 30 pages (16 if scanned), one cached call
  each: ~10 calls, ~$0.30. Each window also gets page 1 and the previous window's end as
  context-only, because a heading on page 2 can govern page 40. A failed window flags review
  and keeps what was read; past 300 pages the rest is flagged. Stress S18: 105/105 rows (the
  old 30-page cap lost 15). Not done: a relevance pass to skip spec-book pages that hold no
  items.
- **The same email delivered twice.** Built two ways. The redelivery hashes to the same cache
  key, so it's free, and `threads` marks the later one `duplicate_of` (stress S13 is a byte copy).
  For real, dedupe on Message-ID plus body hash at the webhook.

## Known broken / next

- `raw` read from pictures varies between runs (E023). The cache makes it stable, not right.
- Thread linking only sees the current inbox; there's no memory of last week.
- The matcher reads only our `description`, so a context miss upstream becomes a match miss.
